a4940.speech: said in a statement issued in Mogadishu to mark World Humanitarian Day: "I pay particular tribute to Somali aid workers who, despite immense challenges, have demonstrated their commitment to serve those in most need of assistance and protection." ; said the theme of this year's WHD, #ActForHumanity, urges the world to do a better job of protecting civilians and humanitarian workers, especially in conflict zones.

a4940.speaker: United Nations
a4940.name: United Nations
a4940.speech: According to the UN, Somalia is experiencing one of the world's most serious humanitarian crises, with millions of people exposed to incredible suffering due to recurring and intensifying climate shocks, protracted conflicts, disease outbreaks, and economic turmoils.

a4940.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a4940.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a4940.speech: said these conditions have led to widespread food shortages and water scarcity, displacement, and proliferation of diseases, and that the need for lifesaving humanitarian assistance and resilience building remains high, despite the number of people in need of assistance having decreased to 6.9 million from 8.3 million in 2023 ; said that aid worker security is a major concern because humanitarian personnel are frequently subjected to violence, both directly and indirectly.

a5059.speaker: New arrivals from the DRC (refugees, unnamed)
a5059.name: New arrivals from the DRC (refugees
a5059.title: unnamed)
a5059.speech: On Wednesday alone, more than 9,000 people arrived fleeing what they described as an increasingly dire situation across the border ; refugees describe fleeing intense clashes and gunfire; many said they did not have enough food to survive and were unable to continue working their land.

a5059.speaker: UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency
a5059.name: UNHCR
a5059.title: the UN Refugee Agency
a5059.speech: Welcomes the Government of Burundi's decision to grant prima facie refugee status to those fleeing the conflict in the DRC, ensuring their swift access to protection and critical humanitarian assistance.

a5059.speaker: UNHCR teams on the ground
a5059.name: UNHCR teams on the ground
a5059.speech: Note a worryingly high number of children among the new arrivals, many of them unaccompanied or separated from their families while fleeing.

a5059.speaker: UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency
a5059.name: UNHCR
a5059.title: the UN Refugee Agency
a5059.speech: Is seeking $40.4 million to strengthen preparedness and deliver life-saving protection and assistance to 275,000 internally displaced people in South Kivu, North Kivu, Maniema and Tanganyika provinces of the DRC, as well as to support a potential influx of 258,000 refugees, asylum-seekers, and returnees in neighbouring countries, including Burundi, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia.

a5059.speaker: UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency
a5059.name: UNHCR
a5059.title: the UN Refugee Agency
a5059.speech: Calls on the international community to support the efforts initiated by the national authorities and humanitarian partners: “Needs are outpacing resources. Without an urgent injection of funds, we risk a further deterioration as the crisis intensifies.”

a5745.speaker: Jens Stoltenberg, NATO Secretary General
a5745.name: Jens Stoltenberg
a5745.title: NATO Secretary General
a5745.speech: Asked South Korea on Monday to "step up" military support for Ukraine, suggesting it reconsider its policy of not exporting weapons to countries in conflict; urged Seoul to do more to help Kyiv, saying there was an "urgent need for more ammunition"; pointed to countries like Germany and Norway that had "long-standing policies not to export weapons to countries in conflict" which they revised after Russian President Vladimir Putin invaded Ukraine in February 2022 ; "If we believe in freedom, democracy, if we don't want autocracy and tyranny to win then they need weapons," he said, speaking at the Chey Institute in Seoul.

a5745.speaker: Jens Stoltenberg, NATO Secretary General
a5745.name: Jens Stoltenberg
a5745.title: NATO Secretary General
a5745.speech: On the war in Ukraine: said it was "extremely important that President Putin doesn't win this war", saying it would make the world a more dangerous place; said it was unclear when the conflict in Ukraine would end, saying Putin was preparing for "more war" and actively acquiring weapons from countries including North Korea.

a5745.speaker: Jens Stoltenberg, NATO Secretary General
a5745.name: Jens Stoltenberg
a5745.title: NATO Secretary General
a5745.speech: On China: said that NATO did not regard China as "an adversary" and believed in engagement on issues from arms control to climate change; NATO allies still trade with China, he said, but added the recent lessons from Europe's vulnerabilities on Russian gas were a key lesson on not becoming "too dependent on authoritarian powers" ; "We are very clear that China poses a challenge to our values and to our interest and to our security and there are many reasons for that," he said, pointing to the crackdown on Hong Kong and Beijing's treatment of minorities in the mainland. "China doesn't share our values. China and the rulers in Beijing they don't believe in democracy, freedom of speech and our democratic values." ; "China is also a challenge because we see that China is investing heavily in mobile military capabilities including long-range missiles that can reach all NATO territory and also this region."

a5745.speaker: Seoul (South Korean government)
a5745.name: Seoul (South Korean government)
a5745.speech: Has said that South Korean law banning the export of weapons to countries in active conflict makes it difficult to provide arms directly to Kyiv, although it has provided non-lethal and humanitarian assistance.

a5745.speaker: Pyongyang (North Korea)
a5745.name: Pyongyang (North Korea)
a5745.speech: Has denied sending weapons to Moscow and said on Sunday that the US would face a "really undesirable result" if it persisted in spreading the "self-made rumour".

a5745.speaker: Kwon Jong Gun, director general of North Korea's Department of US Affairs
a5745.name: Kwon Jong Gun
a5745.title: director general of North Korea's Department of US Affairs
a5745.speech: "Trying to tarnish the image of (North Korea) by fabricating a non-existent thing is a grave provocation that can never be allowed and that cannot but trigger its reaction" ; also called it "a foolish attempt to justify its offer of weapons to Ukraine".

a5745.speaker: Joe Biden, US President
a5745.name: Joe Biden
a5745.title: US President
a5745.speech: Earlier this week promised 31 Abrams tanks, one of the most powerful and sophisticated weapons in the US army, to help Kyiv fight off Moscow's invasion.

a5895.speaker: Save the Children
a5895.name: Save the Children
a5895.speech: Said more than 22,000 people including over 11,000 children have been displaced in Mahaas in central Somalia due to intense fighting that has left thousands cut off without basic services.

a5895.speaker: Save the Children (statement)
a5895.name: Save the Children (statement)
a5895.speech: Said in a statement it is concerned that 21 health sites they support are currently suspended due to the ongoing conflict, including a stabilisation centre for children suffering from severe acute malnutrition, with health facility staff having fled the area, leaving families and children without care ; said that at the time of the escalation in fighting, over 150 children who were receiving treatment for severe acute malnutrition in Mahaas and surrounding villages fled with their families to Bulo Burte and Beledweyne, and that its teams in Beledweyne are trying to trace these children and get them back on treatment.

a5895.speaker: Save the Children
a5895.name: Save the Children
a5895.speech: Said the conflict has resulted in damage to water sources, obstructed road access, and led to a significant increase in food insecurity, with families losing access to grazing land, markets, and clean water ; said it is deeply concerned over increased reports that young boys are being recruited to fight in the conflict by actors on both sides.

a5895.speaker: Save the Children (aid agency)
a5895.name: Save the Children (aid agency)
a5895.speech: Said the recent displacement adds another crisis to a community already battered by a severe drought which has led to a sharp increase in malnutrition, with children lacking access to life saving health services due to aid cuts.

a5895.speaker: Humanitarian partners and local authorities
a5895.name: Humanitarian partners and local authorities
a5895.speech: According to humanitarian partners and local authorities, conflict across central and southern Somalia has displaced about 100,000 people in the Hiraan and Gedo regions in the past two months, placing additional strain on already limited local resources with shortages of shelter, food, clean water, and healthcare.

a6056.speaker: 2024 UNESCO GEM Report, “Lead for Learning”
a6056.name: 2024 UNESCO GEM Report
a6056.title: “Lead for Learning”
a6056.speech: The report explores the key role of leadership in driving educational change ; stresses the pivotal role of leadership in addressing the education crisis, finding that strong, empowered leaders are essential to transforming education outcomes, yet only half of school principals globally receive training in core areas like teaching, collaboration, and personnel development, and that leadership accounts for over a quarter of the variation in school performance, emphasizing the urgent need to invest in leaders at all levels, from ministries to schools ; shows that 251 million are out of school, a mere reduction of 1% since 2015, that numbers of out-of-school children in Africa have increased by 12 million, that 650 million leave school without a secondary school certificate, that the gap between the poorest and richest students’ education completion rates has widened, that the share of official development assistance to education dropped from 9.3% to 7.6% in 2019-2022, that children are less likely to be able to read with understanding today than a decade ago, and that quality standards for teachers are dropping in sub-Saharan Africa as well as in Europe and North America.

a6056.speaker: Manos Antoninis, Director of the GEM Report
a6056.name: Manos Antoninis
a6056.title: Director of the GEM Report
a6056.speech: said: “Good schools require good school leaders who can inject new momentum into learning. These leaders, second only to teachers in influencing student outcomes, must be supported with training and resources. We’re not empowering our leaders to help take education where it needs to be. Four in ten countries do not even give university leaders the ability to take academic and organisational decisions by law”.

a6056.speaker: Education Finance Watch 2024 (EFW 2024) report
a6056.name: Education Finance Watch 2024 (EFW 2024) report
a6056.speech: Cited as the source that for every $100 spent per child in high-income countries, less than $1 reaches children in low-income countries, further exacerbating inequalities, and that low-income countries face overwhelming debt pressures, with six out of ten nations at risk of debt distress, while in Africa countries spent almost as much on debt servicing in 2022 as they did on education.

a6056.speaker: UNESCO
a6056.name: UNESCO
a6056.speech: estimates a nearly $100 billion annual investment gap in developing countries.

a6201.speaker: Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS)
a6201.name: Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS)
a6201.speech: Has continued to express its concerns at the cuts in financial assistance after US President Donald Trump threatened to shut down the United States Agency for International Development (USAID).

a6201.speaker: Winnie Byanyima, Executive Director of UNAIDS and deputy Secretary-General of the United Nations
a6201.name: Winnie Byanyima
a6201.title: Executive Director of UNAIDS and deputy Secretary-General of the United Nations
a6201.speech: Said there is a common feeling that one of the most pressing challenges is the reduction in US support, which could compromise treatment and prevention programmes in Mozambique, as well as around the world. “We talked about how to manage the current situation, due to the changes in US policy, the fact that support will be reduced. We discussed how Mozambique will recover and be able to maintain progress, we discussed various ways of doing this and I believe there is commitment and determination” ; explained there should be a collective approach to discuss with the American government how to make an organized transition, not to stop immediately, but to give Mozambique time to mobilize other resources.

a6201.speaker: Winnie Byanyima, Executive Director of UNAIDS and deputy Secretary-General of the United Nations
a6201.name: Winnie Byanyima
a6201.title: Executive Director of UNAIDS and deputy Secretary-General of the United Nations
a6201.speech: “Mozambique has made a lot of progress, reducing new infections and deaths. However, Mozambique still faces a major challenge, since the country has two million people who are on anti-retroviral treatment, 400,000 still to be taken to treatment, 80,000 new infections every year, so it’s still growing” ; “Progress in the fight against the disease is the result of joint efforts between the Mozambican government and international organizations, but there is still a long way to go. Other solutions include encouraging local production of medicines, reducing dependence on imports and helping to create jobs for young Mozambicans”.

a6201.speaker: Official figures
a6201.name: Official figures
a6201.speech: Indicate that 2.4 million people are living with HIV in the country, reinforcing the importance of continued access to treatment.

a6219.speaker: News reports (2017) on the pollution of water bodies in Ivory Coast
a6219.name: News reports (2017) on the pollution of water bodies in Ivory Coast
a6219.speech: “Bianouan is right on Ivory Coast’s border with Ghana. The source of the Bia River is across the border, in Ghana. And that’s where the problem is coming from. Also, dozens of people are panning for gold near a village called Dadieso in Ghana and this is contaminating the community’s only water source.”

a6219.speaker: Moomaw (2016)
a6219.name: Moomaw (2016)
a6219.speech: Sustainable Development Diplomacy “aims to solve problems through innovative technologies, policies and practices that provide required services by less environmentally damaging means, and implementation of restorative development actions to restore lost ecosystem functions.”

a6219.speaker: Ghana Chamber of Mines (2002)
a6219.name: Ghana Chamber of Mines (2002)
a6219.speech: Cited for the claim that while small-scale mining can contribute to local livelihoods and economic development when conducted responsibly, galamsey often involves illegal extraction of minerals, destruction of natural habitats, and exploitation of vulnerable communities.

a6219.speaker: John Gerard Ruggie (1992), scholar of the liberal institutionalist approach
a6219.name: John Gerard Ruggie (1992)
a6219.title: scholar of the liberal institutionalist approach
a6219.speech: Defines diplomacy as “the institutionalized process of managing relations among states through formal negotiations, diplomatic exchanges, and the adherence to international norms and rules, with the aim of reaching agreements on common action, or at least a common understanding, on matters of shared interest.”

a6219.speaker: Keohane and Nye (1977), ‘Power and Interdependence’
a6219.name: Keohane and Nye (1977)
a6219.title: ‘Power and Interdependence’
a6219.speech: Define bilateral partnerships as “forms of interaction between two units (usually states) that involve some combination of exchanges, mutual benefits, and common purpose.”

a6219.speaker: Dartmouth article (2023), ‘Operation Mercury curbs Illegal Gold Mining in Peru’
a6219.name: Dartmouth article (2023)
a6219.title: ‘Operation Mercury curbs Illegal Gold Mining in Peru’
a6219.speech: Stated that illegal mining had reduced by about 70% since the operation’s inception.

a6276.speaker: United States Agency for International Development (USAID) (press release of 31 October 2024)
a6276.name: United States Agency for International Development (USAID) (press release of 31 October 2024)
a6276.speech: Announced the publication of its new 2024 disability policy, entitled “Nothing Without Us”, which aims to strengthen USAID’s commitment to championing disability-inclusive development and the rights of persons with disabilities; the policy, supported by seven key operating principles, aims to empower and improve the lives of persons with disabilities by ensuring that USAID and its partners recognize, respect, value, meaningfully engage, include and intentionally support them and their representative organizations; under the new policy USAID will update its framework for understanding disability toward a social and rights-based framework aimed at removing societal barriers to participation, promote inclusion in both broader programming and disability-focused activities, underscore the importance of working with persons with disabilities and local PWD-led groups at all phases of the program cycle, and highlight promising approaches to disability inclusion across all its programming areas.

a6308.speaker: Dr Faraja Kristomus, language translator and lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6308.name: Dr Faraja Kristomus
a6308.title: language translator and lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6308.speech: Said the question of the language of instruction in the Education Policy has never been answered because it appears to be a class issue rather than a policy matter; those who decide which language of instruction to use are people of a certain class, while ordinary citizens have not been taken into account; a child from Dar es Salaam can manage English better than a child from Kakonko or Kasulu in Kigoma, because to master a language you must have an environment for speaking it beginning at the family level; Tanzanians fail to speak English because they have failed to strengthen the basic skills of listening and speaking.

a6308.speaker: Dr Faraja Kristomus, language translator and lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6308.name: Dr Faraja Kristomus
a6308.title: language translator and lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6308.speech: Said many Tanzanians encounter English very rarely, from primary school to secondary school, and there is no environment enabling a village child to listen to English so as to speak it; a child begins by hearing his tribal language, then Kiswahili, and encounters English only on reaching secondary school where he is told it is the language of instruction ; said he once carried out an analysis of primary and secondary school examination results for urban and rural students and found rural children failed more than urban ones because urban children had a good environment for learning English.

a6308.speaker: Dr Faraja Kristomus, language translator and lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6308.name: Dr Faraja Kristomus
a6308.title: language translator and lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6308.speech: On teacher preparation, said the teacher who is supposed to teach the child in the classroom does not have language competence and cannot speak English the whole time, so many teachers explain in Kiswahili even the subjects they are supposed to teach in English; "I am not opposed to English, but in order to do justice to the majority of Tanzanians, we policymakers should abandon selfishness by thinking that we ought to make policies that benefit the children of our own class."

a6308.speaker: Dr Faraja Kristomus, language translator and lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6308.name: Dr Faraja Kristomus
a6308.title: language translator and lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6308.speech: On the way forward, said Tanzania has not invested enough in the infrastructure for teaching English, that teachers should be enabled to master the language, that the country should invest in language systems and technology to teach village children and have enough books; proposed programmes to send teachers to the United Kingdom for up to a year of training, the use of colleges of education and universities, and that local councils set aside budgets to send teachers to colleges even for one month.

a6308.speaker: Dr Faraja Kristomus, language translator and lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6308.name: Dr Faraja Kristomus
a6308.title: language translator and lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6308.speech: On the place of English, said English has three levels - mother tongue, second language, and an outer circle of countries that teach it as an international language, such as Germany, France, Russia, Portugal, Japan and China, which emphasise teaching it because they recognise it is an international language they cannot avoid; said Tanzania's test is that people feel they do not need English because they can use Kiswahili, and that Tanzanians should be encouraged to learn English and other languages because these will enable them to get international opportunities.

a6308.speaker: Professor Charles Bwenge of the University of Florida, United States
a6308.name: Professor Charles Bwenge of the University of Florida
a6308.title: United States
a6308.speech: Did research long ago and explained that many Tanzanians have low enthusiasm for English because they initially saw it as a language of colonialism.

a6308.speaker: Dr Faraja Kristomus, language translator and lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6308.name: Dr Faraja Kristomus
a6308.title: language translator and lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6308.speech: On the 2014 Education Policy, said it could not be implemented because of budget constraints and because it required primary education of six years and basic education up to form four, which would have forced standard six and standard seven leavers into form one at once; said stakeholders saw the current curriculum revisions as flawed because they were directed at experts who have benefited from the existing system rather than at a deeper assessment of the beneficiaries of education, with no involvement of target groups in the villages, and that the policy focused more on the age of students staying in school than on teaching.

a6308.speaker: Research by international organisations such as the World Bank and UNESCO
a6308.name: Research by international organisations such as the World Bank and UNESCO
a6308.speech: Shows that children of developing countries, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, lose a lot of time in school without learning.

a6308.speaker: Recent World Bank report
a6308.name: Recent World Bank report
a6308.speech: Shows that in Tanzania a child who stays in primary school for seven years is as if he stays only three years, because teachers do not finish the curricula and syllabuses.

a6308.speaker: Dr Faraja Kristomus, language translator and lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6308.name: Dr Faraja Kristomus
a6308.title: language translator and lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6308.speech: On vocational education, said the plan is a thoroughly good thing but the challenge is implementation because it requires sufficient investment; said technical schools such as Iyunga (Mbeya), Ifunda (Iringa) and Moshi (Kilimanjaro) were abandoned because their machines were outdated; proposed identifying and fulfilling the needs of those schools rather than merely announcing numbers of schools, training village artisans to deliver 60 percent practical training alongside classroom teachers, budgeting for college artisans to update their knowledge, involving technical college teachers and students in construction projects for hospitals, schools and roads, and adding value to artisans so their products can compete in the market.

a6308.speaker: Dr Faraja Kristomus, language translator and lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6308.name: Dr Faraja Kristomus
a6308.title: language translator and lecturer at the University of Dar es Salaam
a6308.speech: On the World Bank-funded HEET university improvement project, said it is a World Bank loan aimed at helping public universities in science, engineering, technology and mathematics; said it aims at building satellite colleges instead of improving the main campus, which is a challenge because new colleges will require increased admissions while capacity is small; said the project should have directed itself more at teaching infrastructure such as offices, classrooms, laboratories, teaching resources and the students' environment, because these are very worn out and domestic budget capacity is small.

a6455.speaker: Mahmoud Moallim, Director-General of the Somali Disaster Management Agency (SODMA)
a6455.name: Mahmoud Moallim
a6455.title: Director-General of the Somali Disaster Management Agency (SODMA)
a6455.speech: Said Saturday that Puntland President Said Abdullahi Deni rejected a request for the federal agency to evacuate wounded soldiers and deliver humanitarian assistance to civilians in Calmiskaad: “I asked for permission to provide medical care for injured troops and to send humanitarian aid to those in need, but the request was rejected” ; he blamed the decision on Puntland's standoff with President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre.

a6455.speaker: Mahmoud Moallim, Director-General of the Somali Disaster Management Agency (SODMA)
a6455.name: Mahmoud Moallim
a6455.title: Director-General of the Somali Disaster Management Agency (SODMA)
a6455.speech: Compared Puntland's rejection to al-Shabab's blockade tactics, warning that state-level barriers risk denying civilians lifesaving assistance: “How can the federal government deliver urgent aid if some regions are shut off and state leaders themselves become obstacles?”

a6455.speaker: Ubah Abdirashid Mohamed Hirsi, Puntland's Minister of Relief and Disaster Management
a6455.name: Ubah Abdirashid Mohamed Hirsi
a6455.title: Puntland's Minister of Relief and Disaster Management
a6455.speech: Defended the move, accusing SODMA of distributing expired medicine and leftover COVID-19 equipment in past operations, citing Moqokori district in Hiiraan where residents battling al-Shabab had asked for wound treatments but received pandemic stockpiles instead: “Puntland does not need face masks, expired COVID-19 kits or expired medicine like what you took to Hiiraan.”

a6455.speaker: Humanitarian experts (unnamed)
a6455.name: Humanitarian experts (unnamed)
a6455.speech: Warn that if aid delivery is subordinated to political rivalries, frontline communities could be left without essential care.

a6648.speaker: Kassim Majaliwa, Prime Minister of Tanzania
a6648.name: Kassim Majaliwa
a6648.title: Prime Minister of Tanzania
a6648.speech: Praised the ongoing "Holela-Holela Itakukosti" campaign's communication strategy, which effectively delivers accessible, understandable information aimed at protecting the health of Tanzanians and their ecosystems ; delivering his keynote address at the One Health Conference in Arusha, emphasized that the campaign represents the nation's commitment to safeguarding public health and the environment ; "The 'Holela-Holela Itakukosti' campaign slogan has successfully conveyed critical health information to Tanzanians in an easy-to-understand manner-it reflects our dedication to protecting the health of our people and ecosystems. With support from USAID and our partners, we are progressing toward a safer, healthier future."

a6648.speaker: Kassim Majaliwa, Prime Minister of Tanzania
a6648.name: Kassim Majaliwa
a6648.title: Prime Minister of Tanzania
a6648.speech: Highlighted the importance of continued political support, robust international cooperation, and sustainable resource mobilization to ensure the long-term success of the One Health agenda ; underscored his support for the campaign and its broader objective of ensuring global health security and sustainable development.

a6648.speaker: USAID
a6648.name: USAID
a6648.speech: Pledged continued support to bolster health security.

a6661.speaker: Joel Akowanou, director of operations of MCA-Benin II
a6661.name: Joel Akowanou
a6661.title: director of operations of MCA-Benin II
a6661.speech: On the Policy Reform and Institutional Strengthening project: said the findings examined at the start were essentially that the electricity tariff did not really reflect the costs borne by SBEE, so the first issue was to make sure the tariff applied takes operating costs into account and allows SBEE to be viable; "We also found that in the sector, regulation was not at the heart of the energy arrangement, in the sense that in any energy system you need a strong and operational regulatory authority"; another finding related to the environmental framework, the environment having to be conducive to bringing private investors into the sector.

a6661.speaker: Joel Akowanou, director of operations of MCA-Benin II
a6661.name: Joel Akowanou
a6661.title: director of operations of MCA-Benin II
a6661.speech: On the Electricity Generation project: said the programme's achievements centre on supporting the government in the process that made it possible to recruit an independent power producer, up to commercial closing, with financial closing now under way; the supporting activities were securing the land for the four solar plants at Bohicon (15 MWh), Parakou (15 MWh), Djougou (10 MWh) and Natitingou (10 MWh), including compensation of people affected by the project, the recruitment of a transaction adviser, and studies to allow the tender documents to be issued.

a6661.speaker: Former Beninese minister (cited by Joel Akowanou)
a6661.name: Former Beninese minister (cited by Joel Akowanou)
a6661.speech: Said that "we have museums instead of investments worthy of the name" in the electric power sub-sector.

a6661.speaker: Joel Akowanou, director of operations of MCA-Benin II
a6661.name: Joel Akowanou
a6661.title: director of operations of MCA-Benin II
a6661.speech: On the Electricity Distribution component: said that until this period there had been no major investment in Benin's electric power sub-sector and that the programme strengthened distribution by building or rehabilitating substations nationwide, building overhead and underground power lines and changing voltage plans, since in the north long distances cause heavy losses; described the major new National Centre for the Control of Energy Distribution (dispatching centre) at Abomey-Calavi, "an electrical control tower" allowing real-time remote operation, network reconfiguration and demand planning, with a backup centre at Bohicon; said the programme also drafted manuals and commissioned a study on network protection made available to SBEE and CEB, because "we had inherited a network that was badly designed, badly sized and badly protected."

a6661.speaker: Joel Akowanou, director of operations of MCA-Benin II
a6661.name: Joel Akowanou
a6661.title: director of operations of MCA-Benin II
a6661.speech: On off-grid electricity access: said the programme first created a regulatory framework allowing foreign investors to carry out rural electrification, citing East Africa where promoters invested heavily and had to withdraw for lack of a framework protecting the State and private promoters; said co-financing was set up to encourage the private sector into rural and peri-urban electrification, with calls for projects covering essential public infrastructure (solar pumps, solar streetlights), mini-grids under concession agreements with the State represented by ABERME, household solar kit sales, and energy efficiency (a private investor's gasifier for his cashew factory); said maintenance and upkeep of off-grid installations is up to the private promoters under the concession arrangement, so the population need not worry; "We have tangible testimonies where people told us: we no longer need to go to Cotonou to watch television."

a6661.speaker: Joel Akowanou, director of operations of MCA-Benin II
a6661.name: Joel Akowanou
a6661.title: director of operations of MCA-Benin II
a6661.speech: On the benefits for the country: said the main benefit is the substantial improvement in the quality of the energy people receive at home, with residents of areas where transformers were installed, notably Vedoko in Cotonou, testifying to a clear improvement in voltage quality, and the managing director of a private company reporting gains of millions of CFA francs after a substation was built next to his factory; said the social component changed lives, as people in rural areas who had never imagined having electricity for another 10 or 20 years suddenly have access, enabling small businesses, mills and television rooms, and that solar refrigerators in remote health centres such as Kalale will now allow vaccines to be preserved and lives saved.

a6661.speaker: Joel Akowanou, director of operations of MCA-Benin II
a6661.name: Joel Akowanou
a6661.title: director of operations of MCA-Benin II
a6661.speech: On the future of the sector: said the energy sector is a vast construction site in which generation, transmission and distribution must each be brought up to standard, and that prospects remain, with a Vinci/SBEE project tackling transmission, an AFD project strengthening transformation capacity and a World Bank project addressing distribution, but there is still some way to go: MCA-Benin II "built the motorways" and now all the access roads must be built to bring the electricity system to a well-sized, well-protected system delivering energy at a reasonable price for the people.

a6740.speaker: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)
a6740.name: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)
a6740.speech: more than 460 million Africans continue to live in extreme poverty, according to the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).

a6741.speaker: Amadou Oury Bah, Prime Minister of Guinea (head of the transitional government)
a6741.name: Amadou Oury Bah
a6741.title: Prime Minister of Guinea (head of the transitional government)
a6741.speech: reiterated the importance of vaccination. “Vaccination attenuates the virulence of a virus through an immediate reaction; this principle is not contrary to our religions or to our customs. Measles is a dangerous disease, so children must be protected. To that end, there is a need to raise awareness among our mothers to vaccinate their children against diseases,” urged Bah Amadou Oury.

a6741.speaker: Oumar Diouhé Bah, Minister of Health of Guinea
a6741.name: Oumar Diouhé Bah
a6741.title: Minister of Health of Guinea
a6741.speech: indicated that the involvement of the transitional government is already showing glimmers of hope in the fight against measles. “This testifies to the government's commitment to the well-being of Guineans. We wish to thank our technical and financial partners, who are essential pillars in our fierce fight against diseases and against deaths preventable by vaccination. Measles is a dangerous and contagious disease; it is responsible for the deaths of thousands of people in the world. It is therefore a scourge that we must fight. According to the WHO, in 2022 an estimated 136,000 deaths were due to measles, most of them children under 5 who could have lived had they been vaccinated. Our country, Guinea, is among the countries of the West African sub-region whose vaccination coverage remains low, and has been so for years, with 47 percent coverage; we must therefore redouble our efforts to reverse this trend and protect our children. The technical strategy includes fixed and advanced vaccination points in the communities, as well as mobile teams to reach areas that are difficult to access,” he declared.

a6741.speaker: Technical and financial partners (WHO, UNICEF, GAVI, Rotary International, Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, CDC, USAID)
a6741.name: Technical and financial partners (WHO
a6741.title: UNICEF, GAVI, Rotary International, Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, CDC, USAID)
a6741.speech: spoke of the dangerous character of measles because of its lethality and its effects, while setting out the arrangements made to vaccinate some 3,705,438 children aged 0 to 59 months in Guinea.

a6741.speaker: Jean Marie Kipela (WHO/partner representative)
a6741.name: Jean Marie Kipela (WHO/partner representative)
a6741.speech: “This mass vaccination campaign is of strategic character for the country and for the region. It is taking place in a particular context in Guinea: the country has recorded more than 2,363 suspected cases of measles, of which 433 cases have been confirmed. These cases mainly affect children aged 9 to 59 months and have been notified in the 38 health districts, 24 of which are currently in a measles epidemic, notably Kankan, Dinguiraye and Siguiri. The WHO recommends routine vaccination and the mass campaign,” indicated JEAN MARIE KIPELA.

a6847.speaker: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of Mali
a6847.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of Mali
a6847.speech: Says it followed with surprise the publication by the United States Department of Government Efficiency, on 15 February 2025, on social media, citing Mali among the countries whose American grants have been cancelled.

a6847.speaker: United States Department of Government Efficiency (social media publication, 15 February 2025)
a6847.name: United States Department of Government Efficiency (social media publication
a6847.title: 15 February 2025)
a6847.speech: Cited Mali among the countries whose American grants have been cancelled, concerning a supposed grant in favour of Mali of 14 million US dollars (about eight billion eight hundred million CFA francs) in support of social cohesion.

a6847.speaker: Government of Mali
a6847.name: Government of Mali
a6847.speech: Recognises itself in the new orientation of the American authorities aimed at cleaning up and humanising their grants, and welcomes this awareness of the reality of their “public aid” and the actions undertaken against its subversive use that does not conform to the essential needs of the beneficiaries.

a6847.speaker: Government of Mali
a6847.name: Government of Mali
a6847.speech: Invites the American authorities to initiate legal proceedings against the persons who diverted the said funds to finance international terrorism, of which Mali and the other States of the AES Confederation are victims; says it should be recalled that Mali, in its quest for sovereignty, has never ceased to denounce, well before the installation of the new American administration, the danger of the diverted use of official development assistance.

a6847.speaker: Malian authorities
a6847.name: Malian authorities
a6847.speech: Hold that international aid is often used as an instrument of destabilisation and subversion of countries through the financing of terrorist networks and as a means of violating the sovereignty of our States; say that in line with the vision of the President of the Transition, Mali has placed all of its cooperation relations within the framework of respect for the sovereignty of the State, the sovereign choices of the Malian people and the defence of their interests.

a6989.speaker: Hakainde Hichilema, President of Zambia
a6989.name: Hakainde Hichilema
a6989.title: President of Zambia
a6989.speech: Has lamented that United States of America President Donald Trump has slapped Zambia on both of its 'cheeks' by withdrawing aid in the health sector, that would now have to see the country strengthen its treasury to procure its own medicines, especially ARVs ; said the return of President Trump into the White House had completely altered the global geopolitics, complaining that Zambia and other African countries should now realise that they were on their own; “Let us not deceive ourselves.”

a6989.speaker: Hakainde Hichilema, President of Zambia
a6989.name: Hakainde Hichilema
a6989.title: President of Zambia
a6989.speech: Has set a target of the country generating up to 1,000 megawatts of solar energy by the end of the year, stating that the feat will be achieved through collaborative initiatives with banks and the private investors.

a7054.speaker: Kristalina Georgieva, International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director
a7054.name: Kristalina Georgieva
a7054.title: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director
a7054.speech: Has cautioned that these trade shifts risk strangling growth in nations already battered by external shocks.

a7054.speaker: UN reports
a7054.name: UN reports
a7054.speech: Foreign aid is projected to fall 18-26 per cent in 2025, equating to US$40-60 billion (E696-1 044 billion) annually less for development and humanitarian needs, according to UN reports.

a7054.speaker: African Union (Ezulwini Declaration)
a7054.name: African Union (Ezulwini Declaration)
a7054.speech: For several years now, the African continent, under the auspices of the African Union (AU), has been pushing for the adoption of the Ezulwini Declaration, from 20 years ago – a call by African countries to have a permanent seat with veto powers in the UN Security Council; the Declaration established a single and unanimous African position on this issue.

a7297.speaker: Ben Kapita, Zambian Agriculture Minister
a7297.name: Ben Kapita
a7297.title: Zambian Agriculture Minister
a7297.speech: Told Reuters in an interview on Tuesday that Zambia will allow 100,000 tonnes of additional white maize exports this year bringing the total to 350,000 tonnes. The move comes after the country recorded surpluses in the last three agricultural seasons, Kapita said. “We are going to export 250,000 tonnes from this year's stock and 100,000 tonnes which should have been exported to Zimbabwe but was kept after Malawi undercut us on the price.” ; Kapita said the maize was ready for export to countries with food deficits, but he did not identify the countries.

a7297.speaker: Ben Kapita, Zambian Agriculture Minister
a7297.name: Ben Kapita
a7297.title: Zambian Agriculture Minister
a7297.speech: Also said Zambia had started to prepare for the 2007/08 farming season with the distribution of subsidised fertiliser and seed to 125,000 small-scale farmers set to start soon. “The government is downsizing the number of farmers getting help because some of them have graduated from the fertiliser support programme. Most farmers are now able to buy their fertiliser from the private sector.”

a7297.speaker: Ben Kapita, Zambian Agriculture Minister
a7297.name: Ben Kapita
a7297.title: Zambian Agriculture Minister
a7297.speech: Last week, Kapita said Zambia's 2006/07 maize output declined 4.4 percent to 1.36 million tonnes compared with output for 2005/06 due to floods which destroyed the crop in 41 of the country's 72 districts.

a7297.speaker: Ben Kapita, Zambian Agriculture Minister
a7297.name: Ben Kapita
a7297.title: Zambian Agriculture Minister
a7297.speech: Said Zambia would keep 250,000 tonnes of maize in strategic reserves compared with a surplus of 160,000 tonnes the previous year.

a7512.speaker: Namibian Association for Private Health Facilities (NAPH) and Namibian Private Practitioners Forum (NPPF)
a7512.name: Namibian Association for Private Health Facilities (NAPH) and Namibian Private Practitioners Forum (NPPF)
a7512.speech: Argue that medical aid funds cannot blame healthcare providers for rising costs while accumulating such large profits.

a7512.speaker: Dr Jürgen Hoffmann, NPPF representative
a7512.name: Dr Jürgen Hoffmann
a7512.title: NPPF representative
a7512.speech: "The surpluses recorded by medical aid funds in 2024 and 2025 show that the problem is not unsustainable service provider costs, but the lack of adequate regulation."

a7512.speaker: Dr Akutu Munyika, NAPH president
a7512.name: Dr Akutu Munyika
a7512.title: NAPH president
a7512.speech: Added that healthcare spending should be directed towards patient care, not surplus accumulation. "Blaming frontline service providers who deal directly with patients, while medical aid funds retain ever-increasing surpluses, misleads the public and undermines trust in the healthcare system." ; Said it was unfair to label doctors, specialists, and hospitals as "cost drivers" when they operate under NAMAF (Namibian Association of Medical Aid Funds) guidelines, which often fail to reflect clinical realities. "The private sector is not the problem – it is part of the solution."

a7512.speaker: Namfisa (latest annual report)
a7512.name: Namfisa (latest annual report)
a7512.speech: Shows that hospitals, pharmacies, specialists, and doctors were the main expenditure items, together totalling N$5.1 billion; hospital claims were the highest at N$1.8 billion, followed by pharmacies (N$802 million), specialists (N$563.2 million), and doctors (N$473.1 million); gross contributions increased by 11.8% to N$6.1 billion in 2024, while claims grew at a lower average of 5.9% over the past five years; open medical aid funds posted a net surplus of N$575.8 million, and closed funds a surplus of N$55.1 million; total assets jumped by 33.4% to N$2.8 billion by the end of 2024, while liabilities reached N$729.6 million; the solvency ratio for open funds improved to 32.1%, up from 24.3%.

a7512.speaker: Dr Jürgen Hoffmann, NPPF representative, and Dr Akutu Munyika, NAPH president
a7512.name: Dr Jürgen Hoffmann
a7512.title: NPPF representative, and Dr Akutu Munyika, NAPH president
a7512.speech: Have called on the ministries of Health and Social Services and Finance to acknowledge that persistent surpluses contradict claims of unaffordable healthcare costs, and urged policymakers to stop "mischaracterising frontline healthcare workers" and instead implement ethical tariffs that reflect the real cost of care.

a7512.speaker: Dr Jürgen Hoffmann, NPPF representative
a7512.name: Dr Jürgen Hoffmann
a7512.title: NPPF representative
a7512.speech: "We need statutory reform, ethical tariffs, and a Medical Control Council to restore fairness and transparency in the financing of healthcare." ; "We are open to constructive dialogue, but continued regulatory failure cannot be allowed to undermine the integrity of healthcare professionals or the rights of patients to ethical, accessible, and sustainable care."
